question: The computer won't turn on at all. What should I check?
ideal_answer_summary: When the computer won't turn on: check the 5V_aux light on the motherboard, verify the voltage selector switch is set correctly (115V/230V), check the power button harness connection to the system board, verify the power cable is connected and the outlet is live, and check expansion cards that might draw too much power. If the 5V_aux light is not on, the power supply may need replacement.

question: What does it mean when the power LED flashes red and the computer beeps?
ideal_answer_summary: Red LED flashing indicates hardware problems: 2 flashes per second with 2 beeps = processor thermal protection (check fan and heatsink), 4 flashes per second with 4 beeps = power supply overloaded/failure (check expansion cards, voltage selector, power supply). These are diagnostic codes that pinpoint specific hardware failures.

question: How do I perform a force-off when the computer is unresponsive?
ideal_answer_summary: To force-off an unresponsive computer, press and hold the power button for at least 4 seconds. This overrides software power control and forces the system to shut down. CAUTION: When resuming from standby mode, do NOT hold the power button more than 4 seconds or the computer will shut down and you will lose unsaved data.

question: The computer shuts down unexpectedly during operation. What might cause this?
ideal_answer_summary: Unexpected shutdowns can be caused by: thermal protection (processor overheating due to blocked vents or failed fan), power supply failure or overload (too many expansion cards), or software issues. Check that the internal fan is operating, vents are not blocked, and the heatsink is properly installed. A red LED flash pattern helps identify the specific cause.

question: What is the voltage selector and why is it important?
ideal_answer_summary: The voltage selector switch on the back of the power supply must be set to match the local AC voltage: 115V for North America or 230V for Europe/Asia. If set incorrectly, the computer may not power on, behave erratically, or the power supply could be damaged. Always verify the voltage selector before troubleshooting power issues.

question: How do I troubleshoot memory problems?
ideal_answer_summary: For memory problems: check that DIMMs are properly seated in their slots, verify memory type matches motherboard requirements (POST error 202 = type mismatch, 213 = incompatible module), run memory diagnostics from DFW, check DIMM configuration (error 214 = configuration warning). If error 201 appears, that indicates a RAM failure — try reseating or replacing the failing DIMM.

question: What should I check if the hard drive is not working properly?
ideal_answer_summary: For hard drive problems: verify data and power cables are firmly connected, check jumper settings (Master/Slave/Cable Select), confirm the drive controller is enabled in Computer Setup under Storage > Storage Options, verify the drive appears in Computer Setup (if not listed it may be a hardware failure), run error-checking utilities in Windows (right-click drive > Properties > Tools > Check Now), and run the Drive Protection System (DPS) self-test from Computer Setup > Storage > DPS Self-test or through Diagnostics for Windows. If DPS indicates failure, replace the drive. For a newly installed drive, try adding a POST delay in Computer Setup > Advanced > Power-On.

question: What does POST error code 101 mean?
ideal_answer_summary: POST error code 101 indicates an Option ROM Checksum Error. This means an expansion card's ROM has failed its integrity check. The solution is to identify and remove or replace the faulty expansion card, or update its firmware.

question: What does POST error code 162 mean and how do I fix it?
ideal_answer_summary: POST error code 162 means System Options Not Set. This typically occurs after a CMOS reset or battery replacement. The fix is to enter Computer Setup (F10 at startup), reconfigure the system options (date, time, boot order, etc.), and save the settings. If the error persists, the CMOS battery may need replacement.

question: How do I reset a forgotten BIOS password?
ideal_answer_summary: To reset a forgotten BIOS password: power off the computer, open the case, locate the password jumper on the system board, move the jumper to the reset position, power on briefly, then move the jumper back to normal position. This clears the stored passwords. The exact jumper location varies by model — refer to the system board label or documentation.

question: How do I clear and reset the CMOS?
ideal_answer_summary: There are two methods to clear CMOS: 1) Using the CMOS button on the system board — press and hold for about 5 seconds with the computer powered off, or 2) Using Computer Setup (F10) — navigate to the CMOS reset option under advanced settings. The CMOS button method is used when the computer won't boot due to a misconfigured BIOS setting. After clearing CMOS, re-enter Computer Setup to reconfigure date/time and boot order.

question: What is the relationship between clearing CMOS and the system date/time?
ideal_answer_summary: Clearing the CMOS resets all BIOS settings to defaults, including the system date and time (this may trigger POST error 163 — Time & Date Not Set). After a CMOS clear, enter Computer Setup (F10) to reset the date, time, and any custom configuration. POST error 162 (System Options Not Set) may also appear because all saved options are erased.

question: The computer was working fine yesterday but today it won't start and there are 4 beeps. What is the full diagnosis and fix?
ideal_answer_summary: 4 beeps with red LED flashing 4 times/second indicates a power supply failure or overload. Diagnosis: 1) Check if any new hardware was added recently that could overload the PSU, 2) Check the voltage selector switch, 3) Remove any recently added expansion cards, 4) Test with minimal configuration (just motherboard, CPU, 1 DIMM), 5) If still failing, replace the power supply. Cross-reference Appendix A LED codes and Chapter 2 Power Supply Problems section.

This is expected behavior after using the password reset jumper — it's not a separate problem but a normal consequence of the reset procedure.

question: Walk me through the complete process of diagnosing processor thermal problems from symptom to fix.
ideal_answer_summary: Complete thermal diagnosis: 1) Symptoms: unexpected shutdowns, red LED flashing 2x/sec with 2 beeps, 2) Verify: check the LED pattern to confirm thermal protection (Appendix A), 3) Physical inspection: ensure CPU heatsink is properly seated with thermal compound, ensure the system fan is operational, check that case vents are not blocked, 4) Remediation: reseat the heatsink with fresh thermal compound, replace the fan if not spinning, improve case ventilation, 5) Verify: run DFW thermal diagnostics after fix.

question: What safety warnings does the guide include and when do they apply?
ideal_answer_summary: The guide includes two types of safety annotations: WARNING (failure to follow could result in bodily harm or loss of life) — applies to electrical work and internal component handling, and CAUTION (failure to follow could result in damage to equipment or loss of information) — applies to procedures like standby resume (don't hold power button >4 seconds), CMOS clearing, and hardware installation. The distinction is critical: WARNINGs are personal safety issues, CAUTIONs are data/equipment risks.
